content.title: National Security Agency | NSA History, Jobs & Role | Study.com
content.text: The history of the NSA can be traced back to the Second World War. During the war, the U.S. Army created a Signal Intelligence Service (SIS) to intercept enemy communications and decode them. This decoding and cryptology work would eventually lead to the creation of the NSA. After the war, there was a realization of the need for a distinct and permanently organized agency to collect, analyze, and protect communications security information. This led to the creation of the National Security Agency in 1952 by President Harry S. Truman. The agency is a part of the Department of Defense and reports to the Director of National Intelligence. Throughout its history, the NSA has played key roles in protecting the United States from foreign threats. During the Vietnam War, several cryptography systems were implemented to protect U.S. military communications. The agency also played a large role in the Cold War, providing intelligence on foreign countries as well as counterintelligence and signals intelligence operations against them. For example, the NSA helped discover the extent of the Soviet Union's nuclear weapons arsenal as well as the missile build-up that led to the Cuban Missile Crisis. One of the big turning points for the agency occurred in the aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001. At this time, the internet and digital communications were becoming much more widespread, creating a need for the NSA to adapt to these new technologies. This led to a dramatic expansion of the agency's surveillance and intelligence-gathering capabilities with a focus on large-scale data mining and analysis of various digital communications.
